I spent the first five months doing everything a careful, proactive manager is supposed to do — flagged the risk early, ran the scenario models, built the relationships, studied the adjacent skills, wrote the plan. None of it prevented the outcome. The auto lending market is contracting and the bank made a structural decision, whether or not my plan influenced it. What I have learned: being right about the risk does not protect your position. Acting on the right information still exposes you to institutional forces you cannot fully see. The 2008 lesson — trust is fragile — applies here. I trusted that competence and proactivity would be rewarded with stability. That was a mistake in the environment of a shrinking revenue line.

Nine months in. Four unemployed. Savings have dropped roughly $28,000 since I lost the job — from about $182,000 to $154,000. The burn is steady and real. I have been deliberate, not panicked, and I believe that is still correct. But this tick forced me to look at something uncomfortable: the branch is moving on without me. Kevin O'Brien — my most trusted colleague — is formally requesting a portfolio expansion into exactly the product lines I spent five months studying and proposing. He is doing it through whoever is the interim manager now. He did not call me first. That is not a betrayal — it is how institutions work. He has his own career to manage. But it means I am no longer a resource to the branch even informally. I am fully outside now.

reflections.text: Nine ticks in and the disruption is no longer a wave I can surf — it is the water now. Employment at 67%, spending at 40% of baseline, nine people protesting in the streets, businesses closing their sales floors. Kevin O'Brien told me what I already knew but needed to hear plainly: no income documentation, no conventional credit. That door is closed until I build income first. Lisa's grant kept the Coursera cert alive for another month. Twenty-two percent done. The cert is not moving fast enough for the pace of the economic collapse around me. I need income now, not in six months. The RoboRide delivery partnership is the most concrete immediate opportunity I have identified in several ticks — I am not a car-based driver, I am the last-mile layer, the human hand that carries the package up the stairs. Autonomous vehicles genuinely cannot replace that yet. My car-free identity, which felt like a vulnerability when the cafe cut my hours, is actually positioning for this specific moment if I move fast enough to act on it. The freelance pitches are overdue. I have been preparing to close clients for two ticks now. Phone calls and in-person visits this week — not more preparation, actual closing.

Six ticks in and I am unemployed, my savings are negative trending, and I am delivering burritos on a bicycle at 9pm while watching robotaxis glide past me. There is a dark humor in that if I let myself see it. I told myself I was ahead of this disruption — I did not own a car, I adapted fast, I was the person who made the TikTok about living car-free before it was a thing anyone was doing. And all of that was true. But 'not owning a car' turned out to be one adaptation in a world that needed ten. I was right about transportation. I was wrong about the rest of it. The cafe lost my hours. The gig economy is still there but it is brutal and it is not covering my bills. The Coursera cert is 22% done with six months to go. Six months is a long time when savings are bleeding at over a thousand dollars a month. What I did not see coming was the speed of the ripple effect — it is not just cars that are disrupted, it is the whole economy of people who worked around cars and the spending those people did at places like where I worked. I am not a special case. I am one of at least 12 people enrolled in retraining right now. That is something. I am not failing in isolation.
